newsitem.title: USA: US stocks end modestly higher, early gains shaved - May 14.
newsitem.headline: US stocks end modestly higher, early gains shaved - May 14.

text.p: U.S. stocks rose modestly on Wednesday after profit-taking unraveled early strong gains after a report showed April wholesale prices posted their biggest decline in nearly four years.

The report signaled the economy continues to grow with few signs of outright inflation and sent the bond market soaring. Wall Street, which had expected April prices to come in unchanged, was caught offguard by the 0.6 percent decline.
The report sent the Dow Jones industrial average soaring 77 points in early trading, but a bout of late-day profit-taking sheared nearly all of the average's early gains.

The 30-stock average closed up 12 to 7286 after hitting a new intraday high of 7351 and spending most of the day above 7300. The Standard & Poor's 500 index also closed higher, up three to 836, but below its earlier new all-time high of 841.
On the broader market, advancing stocks outnumbered falling stocks by 1472 to 992 on volume of about 503 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The April producer price report, released before the market open, sent bonds soaring as investors bet the Federal Reserve would have fewer motives to tighten credit rates at its May 20 meeting on U.S. monetary policy.

The long bond rose a half point, knocking the yield to 6.88 percent after the release of April Producer Price Index (PPI). Lower food and energy costs led the decline, according to the U.S. Labor Department.
Excluding the prices of food and energy, which can vary widely month to month, prices fell 0.1 percent in April.

But stock market analysts said profit-taking ahead of Thursday's release of the April Consumer Price Index (CPI) plus a growing realization that the Fed may still raise rates next week cut into the early rally.

"If (Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan) wants to be pre-emptive against inflation and sneak some tightenings in before the next downturn, he's going to do it even if this week's data is benign," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer of Value Line's Asset Management division.
But although Wall Street may be bracing for another rise in interest rates next week, analysts remains confident that the Fed is not about to embark on a long-term cycle of rate increases.
"The Fed is going to be hard-pressed to continue raising rates," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell chief economist Edward Yardeni.
Yardeni said he had just raised his year-end Dow target to 8,000 from 7,600 and he expects 1997 corporate profits of ten percent, up from his previous forecast of eight percent.
Advancing issues beat losers on the New York Stock Exchange about 5 to 3 with volume at about 502.8 million.
Late day profit-taking knocked the wind out of the Dow and meant the New York Stock Exchange had to lift curbs on arbitrage trading, reinstate them, and lift them again within thirty minutes.

Interest-rate sensitive bank stocks surged amid the benign inflation news and strong bond market. J.P. Morgan & Co Inc jumped 2-1/2 to 104-1/2, BankAmerica Corp rose 4 to 120-7/8, and Citicorp added 2-3/8 to 120-1/2.

Intel Corp rose 3/8 to 152-3/4, a slight rebound from Tuesday's steep losses after the chipmaker said its technology did not violate any patents and it would vigorously defend itself in a patent infringment lawsuit filed by rival Digital Equipment Corp.

Rambus Inc's initial public offering soared 150 percent, closing up 18-1/4 to 30-1/4. Its technology allows semiconductor chips to process data up to four times faster than currently possible, which could speed the graphics-handling capacity of personal computers.

Tiffany & Co shares hit a new all-time high of 45-3/4 after the luxury goods retailer posted strong first quarter profits, driven by overseas demand, especially in Japan. Shares closed up 1-5/8 to 45.
The S&P 500 rose 2.91 to 836.04.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.96 to 1335.55.
Volume on the NYSE was 498.7 million shares.
((-- Wall Street Desk, 212-859-1881))
